topics.title: Shape travels with the data
topics.body: A nested list becomes an array with a shape, and that shape is what every later operation reads. Printing the values and the shape together is the fastest sanity check.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a.shape)
print(a.sum())

topics.title: Subtraction and multiplication are elementwise
topics.body: Arithmetic operators match positions, not rows or columns: `a - b` subtracts the value in the same cell. Shape compatibility is checked before any value is touched.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30])
b = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print((a - b).tolist())
print((a * b).tolist())

topics.title: An array of strings is still an array
topics.body: Text arrays work too, with a fixed-width Unicode dtype. You can slice, sort and compare them, but arithmetic needs a conversion first.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
names = np.array(['ada', 'bob', 'cy'])
print(names.dtype, names.size)
print(names[::-1].tolist())

topics.title: tolist detaches the result
topics.body: `.tolist()` returns plain Python objects, so changing that list cannot change the array. It is the boundary where NumPy values become JSON-ready data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
plain = a.tolist()
plain[0] = 99
print(a.tolist(), plain)

topics.title: A boolean result is a normal array
topics.body: A comparison gives a bool array with the same shape, and that array can be stored, counted or reused. It is not a special object.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
marks = np.array([35, 72, 48, 90])
passed = marks >= 50
print(passed.tolist())
print(int(passed.sum()))

topics.title: Reshaping a list of lists
topics.body: A nested list already carries rows, so `np.array` keeps two axes. Asking for a different grouping is then a reshape, not a rebuild.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]])
print(a.shape)
print(a.reshape(2, 3).tolist())

topics.title: strides report bytes per axis step
topics.body: strides is a tuple of byte offsets: moving one step along an axis jumps that many bytes. For a C-contiguous int64 matrix the row stride is the row width in bytes.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6, dtype=np.int64).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.strides)
print(a.shape)

topics.title: A transpose keeps the same size
topics.body: Transposing swaps the axes and reverses the strides, but the number of elements is unchanged. That is why a transpose is a view, not a copy.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.T.shape, a.T.size, a.size)
print(a.T.strides)

topics.title: dtype name versus dtype kind
topics.body: `str(dtype)` gives the full name like `int64`, while `.kind` gives one character such as `i` or `f`. Kind is what you branch on when the width should not matter.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(str(np.array([1]).dtype), np.array([1]).dtype.kind)
print(str(np.array([1.0]).dtype), np.array([1.0]).dtype.kind)

topics.title: size is zero when any axis is zero
topics.body: One empty axis makes the whole array hold nothing, even if the other axes are large. Plotting or reshaping such an array produces an empty result rather than an error.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((0, 5))
print(a.shape, a.size, a.nbytes)

topics.title: flags report the memory layout
topics.body: `flags` answers whether the buffer is C-contiguous, Fortran-contiguous or writeable. Library calls that require a layout look at exactly these flags.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.flags['C_CONTIGUOUS'], a.flags['F_CONTIGUOUS'], a.flags['WRITEABLE'])

topics.title: base links a view to its source
topics.body: A view's `.base` points at the array that owns the buffer, while an owning array reports None. That single attribute tells you whether a write will be visible elsewhere.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a.base is None)
print(a[1:3].base is a)

topics.title: diag builds a matrix from a vector
topics.body: `np.diag` turns a vector into a matrix with those values on the diagonal, and given a matrix it extracts that diagonal back out.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.diag([1, 2, 3]).tolist())
print(np.diag(np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)).tolist())

topics.title: tril and triu keep one triangle
topics.body: `tril` zeroes everything above the diagonal and `triu` zeroes everything below it. Both accept an offset to move the boundary.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((3, 3), dtype=int)
print(np.tril(a).tolist())
print(np.triu(a, 1).sum())

topics.title: repeat repeats each element
topics.body: `np.repeat` duplicates individual values in place, so `[1, 2]` repeated twice becomes `[1, 1, 2, 2]`. It is different from tiling the whole sequence.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.repeat([1, 2], 2).tolist())
print(np.repeat([1, 2], [3, 1]).tolist())

topics.title: tile repeats the whole block
topics.body: `np.tile` copies the entire sequence as a unit, so a pair tiled twice becomes the pair twice. The output length is the input length times the repeat count.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.tile([1, 2], 2).tolist())
print(np.tile([[1], [2]], (1, 2)).tolist())

topics.title: logspace spaces powers of ten
topics.body: `np.logspace(start, stop, n)` returns values evenly spaced on a log scale, which is how learning rates and frequencies are sampled.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.logspace(0, 2, 3).tolist())
print(np.logspace(0, 1, 3, base=2).round(3).tolist())

topics.title: fromfunction builds from indices
topics.body: `np.fromfunction` calls a function once per index tuple, so a grid can be written as an expression of its row and column numbers.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
grid = np.fromfunction(lambda i, j: i * 10 + j, (2, 3))
print(grid.tolist())

topics.title: Casting to a wider type is lossless
topics.body: Moving from a smaller integer to a wider one preserves every value, which is why int32 → int64 is safe and the reverse is not.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.int8)
print(a.astype(np.int64).dtype, int(a.astype(np.int64).sum()))

topics.title: Booleans cast back to integers
topics.body: Casting a bool array to int gives exactly 1 and 0, which is why boolean counts and arithmetic masks compose.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.array([True, False, True])
print(m.astype(int).tolist(), int(m.astype(int).sum()))

topics.title: float32 keeps fewer digits
topics.body: float32 stores about seven significant digits against float64's fifteen. Printing a float32 array shows the shorter precision directly.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.234567890123], dtype=np.float32)
print(a, a.dtype)

topics.title: int8 has a small range
topics.body: An int8 holds only -128 to 127, so a counter that grows past that wraps. Checking `np.iinfo` before choosing a narrow type is the cheap safeguard.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
info = np.iinfo(np.int8)
print(info.min, info.max)
print((np.array([127], dtype=np.int8) + 1)[0])

topics.title: astype accepts a dtype string
topics.body: The dtype argument can be an object or a short string like `'f4'` or `'int32'`, which keeps conversions readable in configuration-driven code.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(3).astype('f4').dtype)
print(np.arange(3).astype('int16').dtype)

topics.title: promote_types compares two dtypes
topics.body: `np.promote_types` returns the smallest dtype that can represent both inputs, which is the question to ask before mixing arrays in an expression.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.promote_types('int8', 'int16'))
print(np.promote_types('float32', 'int64'))

topics.title: Negative row index selects from the end
topics.body: Rows follow the same negative rule as vectors: `-1` is the last row and `-2` the one before it, regardless of how many rows exist.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(3, 2)
print(a[-1].tolist())
print(a[-2].tolist())

topics.title: Index a three-dimensional array
topics.body: Each axis takes one index, so three numbers address one scalar. Leaving an axis as a colon keeps it in the result.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4)
print(a[1, 2, 3])
print(a[1, 2].shape, a[1].shape)

topics.title: Select rows with a boolean list
topics.body: A boolean list of row flags behaves exactly like a boolean mask and keeps the rows where it is True, in order.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(3, 2)
print(a[[True, False, True]].tolist())

topics.title: take along rows
topics.body: `np.take` defaults to the flattened array, so pass `axis=0` to select rows by position and keep the column axis.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(3, 2)
print(np.take(a, [2, 0], axis=0).tolist())

topics.title: Index with an empty list
topics.body: An empty index list returns an empty array with the remaining axes intact, which is useful when a selection can legitimately be empty.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(3, 2)
print(a[[]].shape, a[[]].size)

topics.title: Read a column as a column
topics.body: A list index keeps the axis, so `a[:, [1]]` is (rows, 1) while `a[:, 1]` is (rows,). The 2-D form is what broadcasts against a row.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(3, 2)
print(a[:, 1].shape, a[:, [1]].shape)

topics.title: Slice with a negative start
topics.body: A negative start counts from the end and the stop still excludes its position, so `a[-3:-1]` keeps two values ending before the last one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[-3:-1].tolist())
print(a[-2:].tolist())

topics.title: Slice a three-dimensional array
topics.body: Every axis can take its own slice, so a 3-D array is narrowed one axis at a time without loops.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4)
print(a[:, 1, :].shape)
print(a[0, :, 1].tolist())

topics.title: Assign a scalar to a slice
topics.body: A scalar on the right of a slice assignment fills every selected cell at once, which is how a block is cleared or reset.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
a[1:4] = 0
print(a.tolist())

topics.title: Assign an array to a slice
topics.body: An array on the right must match the slice's shape. The values are copied position by position into the same buffer.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros(4, dtype=int)
a[1:3] = np.array([7, 8])
print(a.tolist())

topics.title: Slice with an omitted stop
topics.body: Leaving the stop empty means "to the end", so one number plus a colon is enough for a tail. Omitting both bounds copies the whole axis as a view.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a[3:].tolist())
print(a[:].tolist())

topics.title: Slice every other column
topics.body: A step on the column axis samples alternate features in one expression, and the row axis stays untouched.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
print(a[:, ::2].tolist())

topics.title: reshape groups values in C order
topics.body: Reshaping walks the buffer left to right, then down, so a flat `0..5` becomes `[[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]`. The order is C by default.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a.reshape(2, 3).tolist())
print(a.reshape(3, 2).tolist())

topics.title: ravel returns a flat view
topics.body: ravel flattens without copying when the layout allows it, so the result may share memory with the source. Check with shares_memory before mutating it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.ravel().tolist(), np.shares_memory(a, a.ravel()))

topics.title: flatten returns a copy
topics.body: flatten always allocates, so the result is independent of the source. That is the safe choice when a helper expects to modify its input.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4).reshape(2, 2)
f = a.flatten()
f[0] = 99
print(a.tolist(), f.tolist())

topics.title: concatenate along columns
topics.body: With `axis=1`, concatenate joins matching rows side by side, so the row count must agree and the column counts add.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=int)
b = np.ones((2, 1), dtype=int)
print(np.concatenate([a, b], axis=1).tolist())

topics.title: split into equal parts
topics.body: `np.split` divides an array along an axis when the length divides evenly; otherwise use array_split, which allows unequal pieces.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
parts = np.split(np.arange(6), 3)
print([p.tolist() for p in parts])

topics.title: transpose a three-dimensional array
topics.body: `transpose` accepts an axis order, so a (2, 3, 4) block can become (4, 2, 3) without touching the values in memory.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 3, 4))
print(a.transpose(2, 0, 1).shape)

topics.title: maximum picks elementwise winners
topics.body: `np.maximum(a, b)` returns the larger value at each position, which is a clamp against another array rather than against constants.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.maximum([1, 5, 2], [3, 2, 9]).tolist())

topics.title: minimum pairs the same way
topics.body: `np.minimum` is the elementwise counterpart, useful for capping values by a per-row limit array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.minimum([1, 5, 2], [3, 2, 9]).tolist())

topics.title: divide warns on zero
topics.body: True division by zero returns inf or nan and raises a runtime warning instead of stopping the program. Check the mask first when zeros are possible.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
with np.errstate(divide='ignore'):
    print((np.array([1.0, 0.0]) / 0).tolist())

topics.title: power raises elementwise
topics.body: `np.power(a, b)` applies the exponent position by position, so each cell can have its own power while one call does the work.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.power([2, 3, 4], [2, 2, 1]).tolist())

topics.title: hypot is a stable length
topics.body: `np.hypot(x, y)` computes the hypotenuse without intermediate overflow, which the direct `sqrt(x**2 + y**2)` can hit on large values.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.hypot([3, 5], [4, 12]).tolist())

topics.title: ufuncs accept out=
topics.body: A ufunc can write into a preallocated output, so a hot loop reuses one buffer instead of allocating a new array per step.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4.0)
out = np.empty_like(a)
np.sqrt(a, out=out)
print(out.tolist())

topics.title: broadcast_to makes the shape explicit
topics.body: `np.broadcast_to` returns a read-only view of the stretched shape without copying, which is how you inspect what a broadcast will look like.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
v = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(np.broadcast_to(v, (2, 3)).tolist())

topics.title: Trailing dimensions must match
topics.body: Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right, so a length-3 axis can only meet another length-3 axis or a length-1 axis.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
print((a * np.array([1, 2, 3])).shape)
print((a * np.array([[1], [2]])).shape)

topics.title: keepdims prepares a column for broadcast
topics.body: Keeping the reduced axis as length 1 gives a shape that divides back into the original, so normalising rows needs no reshape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1.0, 3.0], [2.0, 6.0]])
totals = a.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
print((a / totals).tolist())

topics.title: A matrix broadcasts with a scalar
topics.body: A scalar needs no shape at all and stretches to every cell, which is why scaling a whole matrix is one multiplication.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print((np.ones((2, 2)) * 3).tolist())

topics.title: Outer difference via newaxis
topics.body: Turning one vector into a column and the other into a row produces every pairwise difference in one subtraction.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print((np.array([1, 2])[:, None] - np.array([1, 2])).tolist())

topics.title: A broadcast error names the shapes
topics.body: The ValueError message reports the operands' shapes, so read it right to left to find the axis that cannot stretch.

topics.title: sum with keepdims keeps the axis
topics.body: `keepdims=True` leaves the reduced axis as length 1 instead of deleting it, which is exactly what later broadcasting needs.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.sum(axis=1).shape, a.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True).shape)

topics.title: quantile uses fractions
topics.body: `np.quantile` is percentile on a 0–1 scale: the median is 0.5. Use it when the requested cut is naturally a fraction.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0])
print(np.quantile(a, 0.5), np.quantile(a, [0.25, 0.75]).tolist())

topics.title: argmax with an axis
topics.body: On a matrix, `argmax(axis=1)` gives the winning column for every row, so the output has one index per row.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9, 2], [8, 3, 4]])
print(a.argmax(axis=1).tolist())
print(a.argmax(axis=0).tolist())

topics.title: cumulative sum along a row
topics.body: `cumsum(axis=1)` returns a running total within each row, keeping the matrix shape instead of flattening it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a.cumsum(axis=1).tolist())

topics.title: average accepts a weight per value
topics.body: `np.average` with `weights` computes a weighted mean and can return the weighted sum with `returned=True`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.average([1, 3], weights=[3, 1]))
print(np.average([1, 3], weights=[3, 1], returned=True)[1])

topics.title: ptp is max minus min
topics.body: `np.ptp` reports the range of the data in one call, which is the spread a box plot draws.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(int(np.ptp([4, 1, 9])))

topics.title: nonzero returns the positions
topics.body: `np.nonzero` gives the indices of the True cells, so a mask can be turned back into coordinates for reporting.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([0, 3, 0, 4])
print(np.nonzero(a)[0].tolist())

topics.title: Count matches per column
topics.body: Summing a boolean mask along an axis counts matches in each column or row without a loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9], [5, 5]])
print((a > 4).sum(axis=0).tolist())

topics.title: Select with an isin mask
topics.body: `np.isin` builds the membership mask, and the same mask filters the values, so a whitelist is one expression.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 4, 7])
print(a[np.isin(a, [4, 7])].tolist())

topics.title: Mask a matrix row-wise
topics.body: A mask built from one column can select whole rows, which is how records are filtered by a field.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9], [5, 5], [9, 1]])
print(a[a[:, 0] > 4].tolist())

topics.title: where with two arrays
topics.body: Both branches of `np.where` can be arrays, so a conditional replacement is expressed without an if inside a loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 2])
print(np.where(a > 2, a * 10, a).tolist())

topics.title: Combine masks with and
topics.body: `&` combines two boolean arrays element by element and requires parentheses around each comparison because of operator precedence.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 8, 12])
print(a[(a > 2) & (a < 10)].tolist())

topics.title: sort descending by reversing
topics.body: `np.sort(a)[::-1]` sorts ascending and then walks backwards, which is the shortest correct way to get a descending order.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sort([3, 1, 2])[::-1].tolist())

topics.title: unique with counts
topics.body: `return_counts=True` gives the frequency of every unique value, which is the basis of a value-count table.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
values, counts = np.unique([1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3], return_counts=True)
print(values.tolist(), counts.tolist())

topics.title: searchsorted needs a sorted array
topics.body: `searchsorted` assumes the input is sorted; on unsorted data it returns a position that means nothing. Sort first when the order is not guaranteed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(int(np.searchsorted([1, 3, 5], 4)))
print(int(np.searchsorted([5, 1, 3], 4)))

topics.title: partition with a kth position
topics.body: `np.partition(a, k)` guarantees that the k-th smallest value sits at index k with smaller values before it, without sorting everything.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.partition([9, 1, 5, 3], 1).tolist())

topics.title: lexsort orders by two keys
topics.body: `np.lexsort` sorts by the last key first, so passing (secondary, primary) sorts primarily by the second array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
primary = np.array([2, 1, 2, 1])
secondary = np.array([10, 20, 5, 30])
print(np.lexsort((secondary, primary)).tolist())

topics.title: isin is membership testing
topics.body: `np.isin` returns a boolean mask for membership in another array, which is what filtering against a whitelist needs.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.isin([1, 4, 2], [2, 4]).tolist())

topics.title: ascontiguousarray forces C order
topics.body: A transposed view is not C-contiguous, so a library expecting that layout may copy. Calling it explicitly makes the copy happen where you can see it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3).T
print(a.flags['C_CONTIGUOUS'], np.ascontiguousarray(a).flags['C_CONTIGUOUS'])

topics.title: setflags can make an array read-only
topics.body: `setflags(write=False)` protects a shared buffer: any later assignment raises instead of silently corrupting it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
a.setflags(write=False)
print(bool(a.flags['WRITEABLE']))

topics.title: view reinterprets the bytes
topics.body: `.view(dtype)` re-reads the same buffer with a different element size, which is how int32 data becomes four uint8 channels.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2], dtype=np.int32)
print(a.view(np.uint8).size)

topics.title: nbytes counts the whole buffer
topics.body: `nbytes` is itemsize times size, so it reports memory even when the shape is a view into a larger array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 3), dtype=np.int16)
print(a.itemsize, a.nbytes)

topics.title: negative strides walk backwards
topics.body: A reversed slice gets a negative stride, so no data moves. The view reads the same buffer from the other end.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a[::-1].strides, a.strides)

topics.title: copy is independent of the source
topics.body: A copy owns its buffer, so writes never reach the original. That independence is what shares_memory reports as False.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
b = a.copy()
b[0] = 99
print(a.tolist(), np.shares_memory(a, b))

topics.title: SeedSequence spawns independent streams
topics.body: `SeedSequence(seed).spawn(n)` gives n generators with independent, reproducible streams, which is how parallel experiments avoid sharing state.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
seq = np.random.SeedSequence(42)
a, b = [np.random.default_rng(s) for s in seq.spawn(2)]
print(a.random(2).round(6).tolist(), b.random(2).round(6).tolist())

topics.title: uniform takes low and high
topics.body: `Generator.uniform(low, high, size)` draws floats in a half-open interval, which is the general form of `random()`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
print(bool((rng.uniform(5, 10, 20) >= 5).all()))

topics.title: integers can take a dtype
topics.body: `dtype='int8'` keeps small draws compact, but the range must fit that dtype or NumPy raises instead of wrapping.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
print(rng.integers(0, 5, 3, dtype='int8').dtype)

topics.title: normal takes mean and std
topics.body: `normal(loc, scale, size)` draws from a Gaussian with the stated centre and spread, which is how synthetic measurements are generated.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
print(rng.normal(10, 2, 3).round(2).tolist())

topics.title: shuffle works in place
topics.body: `Generator.shuffle` reorders the array you pass and returns None. Use permutation when you need a shuffled copy instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
np.random.default_rng(4).shuffle(a)
print(a.shape, int(a.sum()))

topics.title: choice takes probabilities
topics.body: `p=` sets the probability of each item, so choice is a weighted sampler rather than a uniform one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
print(rng.choice([0, 1], size=4, p=[0.9, 0.1]).tolist())

topics.title: datetime64 carries its unit
topics.body: The unit (`D`, `s`, `ms`) is part of the dtype, so adding a number without a timedelta is refused while a timedelta keeps the unit explicit.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
d = np.datetime64('2026-01-01')
print(d.dtype, str(d + np.timedelta64(1, 'D')))

topics.title: astype converts integers to dates
topics.body: An integer array can become datetime64 with an explicit unit, which is how epoch seconds enter NumPy without string parsing.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
epochs = np.array([0, 86400])
print(epochs.astype('datetime64[s]').tolist())

topics.title: sort a structured array by a field
topics.body: Passing `order=` sorts records by the named field, keeping id and score together.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rec = np.array([(2, 70.0), (1, 90.0)], dtype=[('id', 'i4'), ('score', 'f8')])
print(rec[np.argsort(rec, order='score')]['id'].tolist())

topics.title: string arrays have a fixed width
topics.body: The longest string sets the dtype width, and shorter values are padded. A longer value assigned later is truncated, not grown.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array(['ab', 'c'])
print(a.dtype, a.tolist())

topics.title: object arrays hold anything
topics.body: An object dtype stores Python references, so it can mix types but loses the compiled speed and needs pickle to save.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 'two', 3.0], dtype=object)
print(a.dtype, [type(x).__name__ for x in a])

topics.title: read several fields at once
topics.body: Indexing a structured array with a list of field names returns a smaller structured array, which is how a project selects columns.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rec = np.array([(1, 2.0)], dtype=[('id', 'i4'), ('score', 'f8')])
print(rec[['score']].dtype.names)

topics.title: masked_invalid masks NaN
topics.body: `np.ma.masked_invalid` masks NaN and infinity in one call, so a reduction skips the broken cells instead of returning NaN.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.ma.masked_invalid([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(float(m.mean()), int(m.count()))

topics.title: filled replaces masked values
topics.body: `filled(value)` materialises the masked array with the masked cells replaced, which is what a plotting or export step needs.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.ma.masked_invalid([1.0, np.nan])
print(m.filled(0).tolist())

topics.title: count counts the unmasked cells
topics.body: `count()` reports how many values survive the mask, which is the denominator behind every masked mean.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[False, True, False])
print(int(m.count()))

topics.title: nanpercentile skips missing values
topics.body: `np.nanpercentile` computes a percentile over the valid values only, so one NaN does not destroy the whole answer.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(float(np.nanpercentile([1.0, np.nan, 3.0], 50)))

topics.title: isinf finds infinities
topics.body: `np.isinf` isolates the infinite cells, which are a different problem from missing data and often come from a division by zero.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.isinf([1.0, np.inf, -np.inf]).tolist())

topics.title: nan_to_num with chosen fill values
topics.body: Passing `nan=`, `posinf=` and `neginf=` keeps the replacement decision explicit instead of accepting the defaults.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.nan_to_num([np.nan, np.inf], nan=-1.0, posinf=999.0).tolist())

topics.title: Preallocate and assign
topics.body: Building an output array once and filling it by index is linear work. Growing with append copies the whole array on every step.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
out = np.empty(4, dtype=int)
for i in range(4):
    out[i] = i * i
print(out.tolist())

topics.title: Avoid repeated np.append
topics.body: `np.append` returns a new array, so calling it in a loop is quadratic. Collect in a list and convert once instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
values = [i * 2 for i in range(5)]
print(np.array(values).tolist())

topics.title: einsum for a dot product
topics.body: `np.einsum('i,i->', a, b)` states the contraction explicitly, which is a readable alternative to dot for simple index algebra.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(int(np.einsum('i,i->', np.array([1, 2]), np.array([3, 4]))))

topics.title: bincount for integer counts
topics.body: `np.bincount` counts occurrences of non-negative integers in one pass and is much faster than a Python Counter over an array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.bincount(np.array([0, 1, 1, 3])).tolist())

topics.title: vectorize is convenience, not speed
topics.body: `np.vectorize` loops in Python under the hood, so it reads like a vectorised call without the performance. Prefer real ufuncs on hot paths.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
add_one = np.vectorize(lambda x: x + 1)
print(add_one([1, 2, 3]).tolist())

topics.title: Chunk a big reduction
topics.body: When a temporary would exceed memory, reduce each chunk and combine the partial results. The answer is identical, the peak memory is bounded.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
parts = [np.arange(i * 100, (i + 1) * 100).sum() for i in range(3)]
print(int(np.sum(parts)))

topics.title: Standardise columns with broadcasting
topics.body: Subtract the column means and divide by the column standard deviations, both shaped (1, n), to standardise every feature in one expression.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1.0, 10.0], [3.0, 14.0]])
z = (a - a.mean(axis=0)) / a.std(axis=0)
print(np.round(z, 3).tolist())

topics.title: One-hot with eye indexing
topics.body: `np.eye(k)[labels]` turns integer labels into one-hot rows without a loop, which is the encoding most models expect.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(3)[[0, 2]].tolist())

topics.title: Moving average with convolve
topics.body: Convolving with a normalised window of ones smooths a series; `mode='valid'` drops the edges that are not fully covered.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.convolve([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0], np.ones(2) / 2, mode='valid').tolist())

topics.title: diff subtracts neighbouring values
topics.body: `np.diff` subtracts neighbouring values, turning a level series into the changes between periods.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.diff([1, 4, 9, 16]).tolist())

topics.title: digitize assigns bin indices
topics.body: `np.digitize` returns the bin index for every value, which is how continuous measurements become categories.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.digitize([5, 15, 25], [10, 20]).tolist())

topics.title: Confusion matrix with bincount
topics.body: Encoding true/predicted pairs as `true * k + predicted` and calling bincount yields a flat confusion matrix in one pass.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
true = np.array([0, 1, 1])
pred = np.array([0, 1, 0])
print(np.bincount(true * 3 + pred, minlength=9).reshape(3, 3).tolist())
